e.etymology: A respelling of Harley, an English surname and place name from Old English hara (hare) plus leah (woodland clearing, meadow).

assoc.t: Harley-Davidson motorcycles (spelled Harley)
Harley Quinn of DC Comics (spelled Harley)

e.etymology: From Hebrew El'azar: el (God) plus azar (helped). In the Bible Eleazar is the son of Aaron who succeeds him as high priest. Lazarus is the Greek form of the same name.
The Spanish and Italian word for pearl, used as a given name much as Pearl is in English.
The Italian form of Marcellus, a Roman family name that began as a diminutive of Marcus, itself probably from Mars, the god of war.
namesakes: Marcello Mastroianni (Italian star of La Dolce Vita)
Marcello Hernandez (Saturday Night Live cast member)

e.etymology: Mostly a respelling of Mason, the occupational surname for a stoneworker, from Old French macon. Mayson also exists as an old surname meaning son of May, a short form of Matthew.
A pet form of Adelaide, Adeline and Adele, all from Germanic adal, noble, and more recently of Addison. It was a common given name in its own right in the 1880s.
namesakes: Addie LaRue (heroine of the novel The Invisible Life of Addie LaRue)

e.etymology: Possibly from Old Norse brandr, sword. It was long confined to Shetland, spread after Walter Scott used it in The Pirate (1821), and came to be seen as a feminine of Brendan.
namesakes: Brenda Lee (singer of Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree)
Brenda Song (actress)
Brenda Walsh (Shannen Doherty's role on Beverly Hills, 90210)

e.etymology: From the New York City borough, named for the Bronx River, which took its name from the 17th-century settler Jonas Bronck.

assoc.t: the Bronx, New York City borough
Bronx cheer, a loud raspberry

e.etymology: From the English surname and place name, Old English ra (roe deer) plus leah (woodland clearing). North Carolina's capital is named for Sir Walter Raleigh.

assoc.t: capital city of North Carolina
Sir Walter Raleigh, Elizabethan explorer
Raleigh bicycles

e.etymology: From rue, a bitter herb long used in medicine, whose name comes from Latin ruta. It is also a short form of Ruth and Ruby, and it rose with Rue in The Hunger Games and Rue Bennett in Euphoria.
namesakes: Rue McClanahan (Blanche on The Golden Girls)
Rue (young tribute in The Hunger Games)
Rue Bennett (Zendaya's character in Euphoria)

assoc.t: Rue, the young tribute in The Hunger Games
Rue Bennett, Zendaya's role in Euphoria
to rue: to regret bitterly
French word for street

e.note: To rue something is to regret it, as in rue the day.

e.etymology: From Old English Eadmund: ead (prosperity, riches) plus mund (protection). It was borne by Saint Edmund the Martyr, king of East Anglia, and by two kings of England.
namesakes: Edmund Pevensie (the brother who betrays and redeems himself in Narnia)
Sir Edmund Hillary (first climber to summit Everest)

assoc.t: Edmund Pevensie of The Chronicles of Narnia

e.etymology: An Italian compound of Gian, the short form of Giovanni (John), and Luca (Luke), the counterpart of French Jean-Luc.
The Portuguese and Italian form of Christian, from Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
namesakes: Cristiano Ronaldo (Portuguese soccer superstar)

assoc.t: soccer star Cristiano Ronaldo

e.etymology: From Breton mael, prince or chief, the name of an early Breton saint and a favorite in France as Maël. Among Spanish and Filipino speakers it is also a short form of Ismael.
e.note: English speakers tend to read it as MAYL, like mail or male; the French and Spanish sound is mah-EL.

e.etymology: From the surname, which comes from Lindsey in Lincolnshire: the old British name of Lincoln (from a word for pool) plus Old English eg, island. It reached given-name use through the Scottish Lindsay clan.
namesakes: Lindsey Vonn (Olympic champion skier)
Lindsey Graham (US senator from South Carolina)
Lindsey Buckingham (Fleetwood Mac guitarist)

e.etymology: From Arabic Na'ila, one who attains or obtains, the name of the wife of the caliph Uthman. In the US it also overlaps with Nyla.
A modern American coinage that joins Ty to the -lan ending of Dylan and Declan, in the family of Tyler and Tyson.
A recent American coinage in the style of Hawaiian names ending in -lani (sky, heaven), close to Leilani, Alani and Kehlani, the name of the R&B singer.
From Dixie, the nickname for the Southern states, first recorded in 1859. Its source is uncertain: perhaps the Mason-Dixon line, perhaps the dix, a Louisiana ten-dollar note.
namesakes: Dixie Carter (Designing Women actress)
Dixie D'Amelio (TikTok star and singer)

assoc.t: nickname for the American South
Dixie paper cups and plates
Dixie, minstrel song and Confederate anthem

e.note: Dixie is tied to the Confederacy; The Chicks and others have dropped the word for that reason.

e.etymology: The name of the Ethiopian princess in Verdi's 1871 opera Aida, created for the story. A separate Arabic name, A'ida, means returning or visitor.
namesakes: Aida (Ethiopian princess in Verdi's opera)
Aida Turturro (Janice on The Sopranos)

assoc.t: Verdi's opera Aida and the Elton John musical

e.etymology: A spelling of Lennox, a Scottish surname and earldom from the district of Lennox near Loch Lomond, whose Gaelic name is built on leamhan, elm.

assoc.t: Lenox china and giftware
Lenox Avenue in Harlem
Lennox heating and air conditioning (spelled Lennox)
singer Annie Lennox, by surname (spelled Lennox)

e.meaning: of the Geats, a Germanic tribe
e.etymology: A spelling of Jocelyn, from Old French Joscelin, a Norman men's name built on the tribal name Gaut (a Geat or Goth). It became a girls' name in the 20th century.

e.meaning: action, deed; the results of one's actions
e.etymology: From Sanskrit karman, action or deed. In Hindu and Buddhist thought karma is the principle that a person's actions shape their future. It is an English word name in the US.

assoc.t: karma, the idea that actions bring their own results
Karma, Taylor Swift song

e.note: Expect karma jokes: what goes around comes around, bad karma, instant karma.

e.etymology: The English name of the evergreen tree, which came through Old French and Latin from Greek kyparissos.

assoc.t: cypress, an evergreen tree

e.etymology: From Arabic Na'il, one who attains or wins. In France, Nael is also a Breton-style short form of names such as Gwenael and Nathanael.
e.note: English speakers tend to read it as NAYL, like nail; the Arabic and French sound is nah-EL.

e.etymology: From the region of Lorraine in northeastern France, medieval Lotharingia, the realm of King Lothar. It came into use as an English girls' name in the 19th century.
namesakes: Lorraine Hansberry (playwright of A Raisin in the Sun)
Lorraine Bracco (actress in Goodfellas and The Sopranos)
Lorraine Baines McFly (Marty's mother in Back to the Future)

assoc.t: region of northeastern France, as in Alsace-Lorraine
quiche Lorraine

e.etymology: From the English and Welsh surname meaning son of Harry, the medieval English form of Henry. Haris, an Arabic name meaning guardian, is sometimes spelled the same way.

assoc.t: Kamala Harris, former vice president, by surname

e.meaning: she who brings happiness; originally voyager
e.etymology: The Latin form of Beatrice. It began as Viatrix, a female traveler, and was reshaped by Latin beatus, blessed or happy.
namesakes: Beatrix Potter (author of The Tale of Peter Rabbit)
Beatrix Kiddo (the Bride in Kill Bill)
Queen Beatrix (queen of the Netherlands, 1980-2013)

assoc.t: Beatrix Potter, author of The Tale of Peter Rabbit

e.etymology: A modern American name that gives David or Dave the -ian ending of Damian and Darian; compare Davion.
From Old Persian Raukhshna, bright or radiant, the name of Alexander the Great's wife, which reached English through Greek Rhoxane and French Roxane.
namesakes: Roxane (Cyrano's beloved in Cyrano de Bergerac)
Roxana (wife of Alexander the Great)

assoc.t: Roxanne, 1978 hit song by The Police
Roxanne, 1987 Steve Martin film

e.note: Expect people to sing the Police song, in which Roxanne is a prostitute.

e.etymology: A diminutive of Mary or Maria, shaped like French Marielle and influenced by Muriel. It is used in English, Spanish and Dutch.
namesakes: Mariel Hemingway (actress in Manhattan)

assoc.t: Mariel boatlift, the 1980 exodus from Cuba

e.etymology: From Turkish aslan, lion. C. S. Lewis borrowed the word for the great lion of The Chronicles of Narnia, which is how most English speakers know it.
namesakes: Aslan (the great lion of C. S. Lewis's Chronicles of Narnia)

assoc.t: Aslan, the lion of The Chronicles of Narnia
